title: The two missing squares
text:
← Puzzles

Sample math puzzle


The two missing squares
Remove the top-left and bottom-right squares from an 8 × 8 chessboard. Can you cover the remaining 62 squares with 31 dominoes, each covering two adjacent squares?






TipHint





Count how many squares of each color one domino covers.









NoteSolution





Every domino covers one black square and one white square. The two removed corners have the same color, so the remaining board has 30 squares of one color and 32 of the other. A tiling would need 31 of each.

title: What makes a path a geodesic?
text: ← Worked notes

title: What makes a path a geodesic?
text:
Compare two circles
The equator lies in a plane through the center of the sphere, making it a great circle. A circle of latitude away from the equator lies in a plane offset from the center. Its velocity changes direction within the surface as you keep to that latitude.
An arc of a great circle minimizes distance over a short enough segment. Along the same arc, the tangent vector is parallel transported. The parallel transport description extends to geodesics in spacetime.

title: Why a random walk spreads like √n
text: ← Notes

title: Why a random walk spreads like √n
text:
Add the variances
Let \(X_i\) be the \(i\)th step. It takes values \(+1\) and \(-1\) with equal probability, so \(\mathbb{E}[X_i]=0\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=1\). After \(n\) steps the position is \(S_n=X_1+\cdots+X_n\). Independence gives
\[
\begin{equation}
    \operatorname{Var}(S_n)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=n.
\end{equation}
\]
The standard deviation is the square root of the variance. That makes the spread \(\sqrt{n}\) steps.

title: Why a random walk spreads like √n
text:
Try it with a coin
After 100 tosses the standard deviation is 10 steps. After 400 tosses it is 20 steps. If you simulate many walks, compare their final positions at 100 and 400 steps. The second set should be about twice as spread out.

title: The stars around Sagittarius A*
text: ← Notes

title: The stars around Sagittarius A*
text:
S2 and the rotating ellipse
S2 takes about 16 years to go around Sagittarius A*. It passed through pericentre, its closest point to the black hole, in May 2018. Changes in its measured position and velocity across that passage helped the GRAVITY Collaboration detect a shift in the direction of pericentre. GRAVITY Collaboration, 2020
For an isolated Newtonian point mass, the direction of pericentre is fixed. General relativity predicts an advance of about 12 arcminutes in S2’s orbital plane each revolution. On the sky, the shift depends on the orientation of the orbit to our line of sight. GRAVITY Collaboration, 2020

title: The stars around Sagittarius A*
text:
What the measurements constrain
Astronomers fit a model to both astrometric positions and radial velocities. Tracking several stars in the same gravitational field improves the estimate of the central mass and helps constrain the amount of matter distributed around it. A four-star fit reported a central mass of approximately \(4.30 \times 10^6\) solar masses. GRAVITY Collaboration, 2022

title: From Kepler to precession
text: ← Notes

title: From Kepler to precession
text:
An ellipse with a clock
Let \(a\) be the semi-major axis, \(e\) the eccentricity, \(P\) the period, and \(t=0\) the first pericentre. The mean anomaly increases uniformly. Solve Kepler’s equation for the eccentric anomaly \(E\).
\[
E - e\sin E = \frac{2\pi t}{P}.
\tag{1}\]
With the central mass at the origin, the position in the orbital plane is
\[
\begin{aligned}
x &= a(\cos E-e), \\
y &= a\sqrt{1-e^2}\,\sin E.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}\]
Setting \(E=0\) and \(E=\pi\) in Equation 2 gives the closest and furthest distances, \(a(1-e)\) and \(a(1+e)\). Move the time slider through equal increments near the start and near the middle of a revolution to see where the star travels further.

title: From Kepler to precession
text:
The relativistic correction
For a test particle around a non-rotating mass \(M\), the leading-order advance of pericentre per revolution is
\[
\Delta\omega \simeq \frac{6\pi GM}{a(1-e^2)c^2}.
\tag{3}\]
In the explorer, both models use Equation 1 for timing. The precessing trace rotates the Kepler ellipse progressively with orbital angle and reaches \(\Delta\omega\) by the end of each revolution. The model uses rounded values \(e=0.884\), \(P=16.046\) years and \(M=4.30\times10^6 M_\odot\), giving \(a \approx 1{,}035\) AU. Its orientation is shown in the orbital plane. The magnification control scales the displayed rotation, while the readout shows the physical advance. GRAVITY Collaboration, 2020

title: From Kepler to precession
text:
Try it
Use Equation 3 to estimate the physical advance with the parameters above. Take \(GM_\odot/c^2 \approx 1.477\) km and \(1\,\mathrm{AU}\approx 1.496\times 10^8\) km. How much would the angle on the screen change after two revolutions with magnification enabled?






NoteShow the calculation





The rounded parameters give \(\Delta\omega \approx 3.5\times 10^{-3}\) radians, or approximately \(12.2\) arcminutes. After two revolutions the physical advance is about \(24.3\) arcminutes. Multiplying by 60 makes the angle on the screen about \(24.3^\circ\).

title: Check a numerical solution by halving the step
text: ← Notes

title: Check a numerical solution by halving the step
section: A problem with an exact answer
text:
A problem with an exact answer
For \(y'=-y\) with \(y(0)=1\), the exact solution is \(y(t)=e^{-t}\). Forward Euler takes steps of size \(h\) using \(y_{k+1}=(1-h)y_k\). To compare runs, keep the final time at \(t=1\) and change only the number of steps.
from math import exp

exact = exp(-1)
for steps in (10, 20, 40, 80):
    step_size = 1 / steps
    value = 1.0
    for _ in range(steps):
        value -= step_size * value
    print(f"{steps:3d} steps   error {abs(value - exact):.6f}")

title: Check a numerical solution by halving the step
text:
Read the pattern
The error goes from about \(0.0192\) at 10 steps to \(0.0094\) at 20 steps. It roughly halves with \(h\), as expected for a first-order method. A useful convergence check keeps the initial condition and ending time fixed so that you can attribute the change in error to the step size.
